answers.label: C
answers.working:
The four resistors form a Wheatstone bridge with the \(5\,\Omega\) resistor as the galvanometer arm. No current flows through the \(5\,\Omega\) resistor only when the bridge is balanced, that is when the ratios of the arms on either side are equal:

\(\dfrac{10}{10} = \dfrac{25}{X}\)

So \(X = 25\,\Omega\). The answer is option (C), \(25\,\Omega\).

answers.label: D
answers.value: ‘X’ is diamagnetic and ‘Y’ is paramagnetic.
answers.working:
A diamagnetic substance is weakly repelled by a magnetic field, so its relative permeability is slightly less than 1. A paramagnetic substance is weakly attracted, so its relative permeability is slightly more than 1. A ferromagnetic substance has a relative permeability much greater than 1 (hundreds or thousands), not slightly more than 1.

So X is diamagnetic and Y is paramagnetic: option (D).

answers.label: D
answers.value: half.
answers.working:
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass \(m\) and kinetic energy \(K\) is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\), so \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}\).

If \(K\) becomes \(4K\), then \(\lambda\) becomes \(\dfrac{\lambda}{\sqrt{4}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\). The wavelength becomes half: option (D).

answers.label: B
answers.value: Reverse the terminals of battery \(E_1\) or \(E_2\).
answers.working:
Two parallel wires attract when their currents flow in the same direction and repel when the currents flow in opposite directions. The wires are attracting, so the currents in MN and ST are in the same direction at present.

To make them repel, the current in only one wire must be reversed, which is done by reversing the terminals of one battery, \(E_1\) or \(E_2\). Reversing both batteries reverses both currents, which keeps them in the same direction, so the wires would still attract. Making \(E_1 = E_2\) or adding a key and ammeter does not change the directions.

So the answer is option (B).

answers.label: B
answers.value: majority of free electrons as charge carriers.
answers.working:
An N-type semiconductor is made by adding a pentavalent impurity (such as arsenic or phosphorus) to pure silicon or germanium. Each impurity atom donates a free electron, so free electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers. A trivalent impurity would give a P-type semiconductor, and equal numbers of holes and electrons describe an intrinsic (pure) semiconductor.

So the answer is option (B).

answers.label: C
answers.value: Assertion is true and Reason is false.
answers.working:
By the lens maker's formula, \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_g}{n_m} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\). In water, \(\dfrac{n_g}{n_w} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}33} \approx 1{\cdot}13\), which is less than \(\dfrac{n_g}{n_a} = 1{\cdot}5\). So \(\dfrac{1}{f}\) becomes smaller and the focal length increases: the Assertion is true.

The Reason says the refractive index of glass with respect to water is greater than with respect to air. This is false: it is smaller (about \(1{\cdot}13\) against \(1{\cdot}5\)), and that is exactly why the focal length increases.

So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: A
answers.value: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
answers.working:
Diffraction is noticeable only when the size of the obstacle or aperture is comparable to the wavelength. The wavelength of light is very small (about \(10^{-7}\) m), while everyday objects are far larger, so light seems to travel in straight lines and diffraction is hard to notice. In the laboratory we use very narrow slits or fine obstacles, so diffraction can be seen.

Both statements are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: option (A).

answers.value: Resistance decreases as temperature increases.
answers.working: The resistance of a semiconductor **decreases** as its temperature increases (it has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance). On heating, more electrons gain enough energy to cross the small energy gap into the conduction band, so the number of free electrons and holes increases and the crystal conducts better.

answers.value: Step-down transformer: \(N_s < N_p\), so \(V_s < V_p\); power is conserved, so \(I_s > I_p\).
answers.working:
The secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary, so this is a **step-down** transformer: \(\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} < 1\).

In an ideal transformer there is no loss of power, so input power = output power: \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\), giving \(\dfrac{I_s}{I_p} = \dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s} > 1\). Since the voltage is stepped down, the current is stepped up, so the secondary current is greater than the primary current.

answers.value: Primary: red on the outside, violet inside (one internal reflection); secondary: order reversed (two internal reflections).
answers.working:
Any one of these:

- In the **primary rainbow** red is on the outer side and violet on the inner side; in the **secondary rainbow** the order of colours is reversed (violet outside, red inside).
- The primary rainbow is formed by **one** total internal reflection inside the raindrops; the secondary rainbow by **two** internal reflections.
- The primary rainbow is brighter; the secondary rainbow is fainter and appears above (outside) the primary.

answers.value: A mirror has no chromatic aberration.
answers.working: A mirror objective is **free from chromatic aberration**, because reflection does not depend on wavelength, so all colours are focused at the same point. (Other acceptable advantages: a parabolic mirror is free from spherical aberration; a large mirror is lighter and easier to support than a large lens of the same size, so a bigger aperture can be used to gather more light.)

answers.value: Electron diffraction (Davisson-Germer experiment).
answers.working: **Diffraction of electrons**, as observed in the Davisson-Germer experiment, where a beam of electrons scattered from a nickel crystal produces a diffraction pattern just like X-rays. This shows that moving particles behave like waves (also used in the electron microscope).

answers.value: \(1{\cdot}02\) MeV
answers.working:
In pair production the photon's energy is converted into the rest mass energy of an electron and a positron, each of which is \(m_ec^2 = 0{\cdot}51\) MeV. So the minimum energy of the gamma ray photon is

\(E_{min} = 2m_ec^2 = 2 \times 0{\cdot}51 = 1{\cdot}02\) MeV.

answers.value: A conductor (metal).
answers.working: When there is no forbidden band, the valence band and the conduction band overlap, so electrons move freely into the conduction band. Such a material is a **conductor** (a metal).

answers.value: (a) Capacitance decreases; (b) capacitance increases \(K\) times.
answers.working:
**(a)** The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is \(C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\), so \(C \propto \dfrac{1}{d}\). If the distance between the plates is increased, the capacitance **decreases** (doubling \(d\) halves \(C\)).

**(b)** With a dielectric of dielectric constant \(K\) filling the space between the plates, \(C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}\). Since \(K > 1\), the capacitance **increases** (by a factor \(K\) when the slab fills the gap). The dielectric is polarised and reduces the field and the potential difference between the plates for the same charge, so \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\) increases.

answers.value: (a) Figure 4 (series); (b) \(\frac{I_1}{I_2} = 2\)
answers.working:
**(a)** In Figure 4 the cells are in series, so the emf of the battery is \(E + E = 2E\). In Figure 5 the identical cells are in parallel, so the emf is only \(E\). The emf is **greater in Figure 4**.

**(b)** The internal resistances are negligible, so the only resistance in each circuit is \(R\).

Figure 4: \(I_1 = \dfrac{2E}{R}\)

Figure 5: \(I_2 = \dfrac{E}{R}\)

So \(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{2E/R}{E/R} = 2\), that is \(I_1 : I_2 = 2 : 1\).
answers.flag: Figure 5 labels the upper cell 'S' (the lower is 'E'); read as a misprint for E, since the stem calls the cells identical.

answers.value: (i) The equatorial plane (perpendicular bisector plane of the dipole); (ii) \(\frac{E_1}{E_2} = 2\)
answers.working:
**(i)** The potential of a short dipole at distance \(r\) is \(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}\). It is zero when \(\cos\theta = 0\), that is \(\theta = 90^\circ\). So the locus of points of zero potential is the **equatorial plane**: the plane through the centre of the dipole perpendicular to its axis (the perpendicular bisector of the dipole).

**(ii)** For a short dipole at distance \(r\):

Axial point: \(E_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}\)

Equatorial point: \(E_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}\)

So \(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = 2\), that is \(E_1 : E_2 = 2 : 1\).

**(a)** Apply Kirchhoff's junction (current) law at junction Q. Currents entering Q: 3 A from P and \(I\) from S. Current leaving Q: 4 A towards R.

\(3 + I = 4 \Rightarrow I = 1\) A (flowing from S to Q through the \(2\,\Omega\) resistor).

(Check with loop PQSP, using Kirchhoff's loop law: \(10 = 4 \times 3 - 2 \times 1 = 10\), which agrees.)

**(b)** Apply Kirchhoff's loop (voltage) law to loop QRSQ. The cell E drives the current from R to S, and the current through the \(2\,\Omega\) resistor flows from S to Q:

\(E = 1 \times 4 + 2 \times 1\)

\(E = 4 + 2 = 6\) V.

(Check with the outer loop PQRSP: \(10 + E = 4 \times 3 + 1 \times 4 = 16\), giving \(E = 6\) V again.)

In a potentiometer the emf of a cell is proportional to its balancing length: \(E \propto l\).

\(\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{l_2}{l_1}\)

\(E_2 = E_1 \times \dfrac{l_2}{l_1} = 1{\cdot}25 \times \dfrac{63}{35} = 1{\cdot}25 \times 1{\cdot}8 = 2{\cdot}25\) V.

The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of \(N\) turns, radius \(r\), carrying current \(I\) is

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2r}\)

When \(I\), \(N\) and \(r\) are all doubled:

\(B' = \dfrac{\mu_0 (2N)(2I)}{2(2r)} = 2 \times \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2r} = 2B\)

The magnetic field at the centre becomes \(2B\) (it is doubled).

answers.value: \(2\) m (\(200\) cm), a converging combination
answers.working:
For lenses in contact, the powers add:

\(P = P_1 + P_2 = (+2{\cdot}0) + (-1{\cdot}5) = +0{\cdot}5\) D

Focal length \(f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}5}\) m \(= 2\) m \(= 200\) cm.

The positive sign shows the objective behaves as a convex (converging) lens of focal length 2 m.

answers.value: (i) Microwaves; (ii) \(5 \times 10^{16}\) Hz
answers.working:
**(i)** Satellite communication (the downlink from the satellite to the dish antenna) uses **microwaves**. They pass through the ionosphere without being reflected and can be sent as a narrow beam aimed at the dish.

**(ii)** For an electromagnetic wave, \(c = f\lambda\), so

\(f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{6 \times 10^{-9}} = 5 \times 10^{16}\) Hz.

answers.value: Definitions of threshold frequency and work function.
answers.working:
**(i) Threshold frequency:** the minimum frequency of incident radiation that can eject photoelectrons from the surface of a given metal. Below this frequency no photoelectric emission takes place, however intense the light is. (\(f_0 = \dfrac{\phi_0}{h}\))

**(ii) Work function:** the minimum energy that must be supplied to an electron to just remove it from the surface of a given metal. It is denoted by \(\phi_0\) and equals \(h f_0\); it is usually expressed in electron volts.

answers.value: (i) \(E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\); (ii)(a) \(\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\); (b) from the \(+\sigma\) sheet towards the \(-\sigma\) sheet (to the right)
answers.working:
**(i)** By Gauss's law, the electric field near an infinite plane sheet of charge with surface charge density \(\sigma\) is

\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

It is uniform (independent of the distance \(r\)) and directed away from the positively charged sheet, that is to the right at P.

**(ii)(a)** At P (between the sheets), the \(+\sigma\) sheet gives a field \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) directed away from it (to the right), and the \(-\sigma\) sheet gives a field \(\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\) directed towards it (also to the right). The two fields add:

\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)

**(b)** The resultant field is perpendicular to the sheets and directed from the positively charged sheet towards the negatively charged sheet (from \(+\sigma\) to \(-\sigma\), to the right).
answers.flag: The stem says 'metallic sheet'. For a thin charged sheet the field is \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) (answered here, as the question clearly intends via part (ii)); for a thick conducting plate with \(\sigma\) on its face it would be \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\).

answers.value: (a) X: ammeter, Y: voltmeter; (b)(1) \(E = 2{\cdot}5\) V, (2) \(r = 5\,\Omega\)
answers.working:
**(a)** X is connected in series with R, so it measures the current: **X is an ammeter**. Y is connected across (in parallel with) R, so it measures the potential difference: **Y is a voltmeter**.

**(b)** The terminal voltage of the cell is \(V = E - Ir\), so the V-I graph is a straight line with intercept \(E\) on the V axis and slope \(-r\).

**(1)** When \(I = 0\) (no current drawn), \(V = E\). The line meets the V axis at \(2{\cdot}5\) V, so **\(E = 2{\cdot}5\) V**.

**(2)** When \(V = 0\) (the cell is short-circuited, R = 0), \(I = \dfrac{E}{r}\). The line meets the I axis at \(I = 0{\cdot}5\) A, so

\(r = \dfrac{E}{I_{max}} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5}{0{\cdot}5} = 5\,\Omega\)

(This is the magnitude of the slope: \(r = \dfrac{2{\cdot}5 - 0}{0{\cdot}5 - 0} = 5\,\Omega\).)
answers.flag: The graph's scale is ambiguous as printed: the V labels 0.5 to 2.5 do not line up with the tick dots, and the label 0.5 sits beside the I axis, as if the axis were at V = 0.5. Read as the line running from V = 2.5 V (I = 0) to I = 0.5 A (V = 0), giving E = 2.5 V and r = 5 ohm. If the I axis really were at V = 0.5 V, the numbers would differ (r = 4 ohm).

answers.value: (a) Wire A; (b) Wire B, because it carries the greater current density for the same E
answers.working:
**(a)** Current density and electric field are related by Ohm's law in the form \(J = \sigma E = \dfrac{E}{\rho}\), where \(\sigma\) is the conductivity and \(\rho\) the resistivity. So the slope of the J-E graph equals \(\dfrac{1}{\rho}\).

Line A has the smaller slope, so A has the smaller conductivity and therefore the **higher resistivity**: wire **A**.

**(b)** For the same electric field E, the graph shows that the current density in **B** is greater than in A. Current density is \(J = n e v_d\), so (for metals with a comparable number density \(n\) of free electrons) a greater current density means a greater drift velocity. Hence the drift velocity is greater in **wire B**. Equivalently, B has the higher conductivity, meaning its electrons are less hindered (larger relaxation time \(\tau\)), and \(v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}\) is larger.
answers.flag: Part (b) strictly needs the two metals to have similar free-electron density n (J = n e v_d); the question gives no n, so B is the intended answer on that assumption.

answers.value: Connect a resistance of \(9980\,\Omega\) in series with the galvanometer.
answers.working:
To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance \(R\) is connected **in series** with it, so that a potential difference \(V\) across the combination sends exactly the full scale current \(I_g\).

Given: \(G = 20\,\Omega\), \(I_g = 1\) mA \(= 10^{-3}\) A, \(V = 10\) V.

\(V = I_g (G + R)\)

\(R = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{10}{10^{-3}} - 20 = 10000 - 20 = 9980\,\Omega\)

So a resistance of \(9980\,\Omega\) must be connected in series with the galvanometer. The scale is then recalibrated to read 0 to 10 V.

answers.value: \(B = 0\) at X
answers.working:
Point X is 2 cm \(= 0{\cdot}02\) m from PQ and \(10 - 2 = 8\) cm \(= 0{\cdot}08\) m from RS. The field of a long straight wire is \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\), where \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\) T m A\(^{-1}\).

Field due to PQ:

\(B_1 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 4}{0{\cdot}02} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\) T

By the right-hand thumb rule, PQ carries current upward and X is to its right, so \(B_1\) is directed **into** the plane of the paper.

Field due to RS:

\(B_2 = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 16}{0{\cdot}08} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\) T

RS carries current upward and X is to its left, so \(B_2\) is directed **out of** the plane of the paper.

The two fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the resultant magnetic field at X is

\(B = B_1 - B_2 = 0\).

answers.value: (a) A circle in the XY plane; (b) \(f \approx 4{\cdot}79 \times 10^{6}\) Hz
answers.working:
**(a)** The magnetic force \(\vec F = q(\vec v \times \vec B)\) is always perpendicular to the velocity, and the velocity (along the X axis) is perpendicular to the field (along the Z axis). So the force does no work: the speed stays constant and only the direction changes. The electron therefore moves in a **circular path** in the XY plane (the plane perpendicular to B). Here \(\hat i \times (-\hat k) = +\hat j\), and since the electron's charge is negative, the force on it at the start is along the \(-Y\) direction, so it starts curving towards \(-Y\).

**(b)** For circular motion, \(qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\), and the time period is \(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\). The frequency of revolution is

\(f = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} \times 0{\cdot}314}{2 \times 3{\cdot}14 \times 1{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-27}}\)

\(f = \dfrac{0{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-20}}{1{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 4{\cdot}79 \times 10^{6}\) Hz

(It does not depend on the speed of the proton.)

answers.value: (i) Between the lens and its focus, at \(u = \frac{fD}{f + D}\) from the lens; (ii) virtual, erect, magnified
answers.working:
**(i)** For a magnifying glass the diamond must be placed **between the optical centre and the principal focus** of the convex lens (closer to the lens than \(f\)). For the image to form at the least distance of distinct vision, put \(v = -D\) in the lens formula \(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\):

\(-\dfrac{1}{D} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \Rightarrow u = -\dfrac{fD}{f + D}\)

So the diamond is kept on the far side of the lens from the eye, at a distance \(\dfrac{fD}{f + D}\) from the lens, which is a little less than \(f\).

**(ii)** Any two characteristics of the image:

- it is **virtual**,
- it is **erect** (upright),
- it is **magnified** (magnification \(m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f}\)),
- it is formed on the same side of the lens as the object.

answers.value: Diagram described; \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \text{constant}\) proved.
answers.working:
**(i) Diagram:** Draw a horizontal line XY as the surface separating the rarer medium 1 (above, speed of light \(v_1\)) from the denser medium 2 (below, speed \(v_2\), with \(v_2 < v_1\)). Draw parallel incident rays meeting the surface obliquely. The incident plane wavefront AB is drawn perpendicular to these rays, with A on the surface and B still in medium 1. The angle between AB and the surface XY is marked \(i\) (equal to the angle of incidence between the ray and the normal). The refracted wavefront CE is drawn from C (where the ray from B meets the surface, so BC is along the ray) as a tangent to a secondary wavelet of radius AE drawn about A in medium 2. The angle between CE and the surface is marked \(r\). Refracted rays, perpendicular to CE, bend towards the normal. Normals at A and C are shown dotted.

**(ii) Proof of Snell's law using Huygens' principle:**

Let the wavefront AB take time \(t\) for its point B to reach C. In this time B travels \(BC = v_1 t\) in medium 1. Meanwhile, by Huygens' principle, A becomes a source of secondary wavelets which spread into medium 2; in time \(t\) the wavelet from A has radius \(AE = v_2 t\). The tangent CE drawn from C to this wavelet is the refracted wavefront.

In right triangle ABC (right angle at B), \(\angle BAC = i\), so

\(\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1 t}{AC}\)

In right triangle AEC (right angle at E), \(\angle ACE = r\), so

\(\sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2 t}{AC}\)

Dividing,

\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\)

Since \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) are constants for the two media, \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}\) is a constant, equal to the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1: \(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = {}_1n_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\). Also the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in the same plane. This is **Snell's law** of refraction.

answers.value: Proved.
answers.working:
Let a ray PQ fall on face AB of a prism of angle \(A\) at angle of incidence \(i_1\), refract along QR at angle \(r_1\), meet face AC at angle of incidence \(r_2\), and emerge along RS at angle of emergence \(i_2\). Let \(\delta\) be the angle of deviation between the incident and emergent rays. Let the normals at Q and R meet at N.

**Step 1 (angle of prism):** In quadrilateral AQNR, the angles at Q and R are \(90^\circ\), so \(\angle A + \angle QNR = 180^\circ\). In triangle QNR, \(r_1 + r_2 + \angle QNR = 180^\circ\). Comparing,

\(r_1 + r_2 = A\) ...(1)

**Step 2 (deviation):** The deviation at the first face is \(i_1 - r_1\) and at the second face \(i_2 - r_2\). So

\(\delta = (i_1 - r_1) + (i_2 - r_2) = i_1 + i_2 - A\) ...(2)

**Step 3 (minimum deviation):** At the position of minimum deviation \(\delta = \delta_m\), the ray passes symmetrically through the prism: \(i_1 = i_2 = i\) and \(r_1 = r_2 = r\). Then from (1), \(2r = A\), so

\(r = \dfrac{A}{2}\)

and from (2), \(\delta_m = 2i - A\), so

\(i = \dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\)

**Step 4 (Snell's law at the first face):** \(n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}\). Substituting,

\(n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right)}\)

Hence proved. (A labelled diagram shows the triangular prism ABC, the incident ray PQ, the refracted ray QR inside, the emergent ray RS, the normals at Q and R meeting at N, and the angles \(i_1, r_1, r_2, i_2, A\) and \(\delta\).)

answers.value: (i) \(1{\cdot}152\) mm; (ii) fringe width falls to \(0{\cdot}12\) mm, fringes come closer
answers.working:
Given: \(d = 5\) mm \(= 5 \times 10^{-3}\) m, \(\lambda = 600\) nm \(= 6 \times 10^{-7}\) m, \(D = 1{\cdot}2\) m.

Fringe width:

\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7} \times 1{\cdot}2}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}44 \times 10^{-4}\) m \(= 0{\cdot}144\) mm

**(i)** The \(n^{\text{th}}\) bright fringe is at a distance \(n\beta\) from the central bright band. The 5th bright fringe on one side is at \(5\beta\) and the 3rd bright fringe on the other side is at \(3\beta\), so the distance between them is

\(5\beta + 3\beta = 8\beta = 8 \times 1{\cdot}44 \times 10^{-4} = 1{\cdot}152 \times 10^{-3}\) m \(= 1{\cdot}152\) mm.

**(ii)** Since \(\beta \propto \lambda\), with \(\lambda = 500\) nm the fringe width becomes

\(\beta' = \dfrac{500}{600} \times 0{\cdot}144 = 0{\cdot}12\) mm.

The fringes become narrower and move closer together (more fringes in the same width); the central band stays bright and at the same place.

answers.value: (i) Straight line with positive slope cutting the f axis at the threshold frequency \(f_0\); (ii) \(h = e \times \text{slope}\)
answers.working:
**(i)** From Einstein's photoelectric equation, \(eV_s = hf - \phi_0\), so

\(V_s = \dfrac{h}{e}f - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)

The graph of stopping potential \(V_s\) (vertical axis) against frequency \(f\) (horizontal axis) is a **straight line** with a positive slope. It meets the frequency axis at the **threshold frequency \(f_0\)**: there is no stopping potential (no emission) for \(f < f_0\). Label the axes \(V_s\) and \(f\), mark \(f_0\) on the f axis, and mark the slope \(\dfrac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta f}\). If the line is extended backwards, it cuts the \(V_s\) axis at \(-\dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\).

**(ii)** The slope of the line is \(\dfrac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta f} = \dfrac{h}{e}\). So Planck's constant is found by measuring the slope from the graph and multiplying it by the electronic charge:

\(h = e \times \text{slope} = e \times \dfrac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta f}\)

answers.value: (a)(1) 3 V; (2) Fleming's right-hand rule (or Lenz's law); (b) \(0{\cdot}4\) H
answers.working:
**(a)(1)** The speed of the rod is \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(\pi t) = \pi\) m s\(^{-1}\).

Motional emf:

\(e = Blv = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \times 3 \times \pi = 3\) V

**(2)** The direction of the induced current is found using **Fleming's right-hand rule** (which follows from **Lenz's law**): stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand mutually perpendicular; if the forefinger points along the field and the thumb along the motion of the conductor, the middle finger gives the direction of the induced current.

**(b)** The induced emf in a coil is \(e = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\) (in magnitude).

\(\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{15 - 0}{0{\cdot}2} = 75\) A s\(^{-1}\)

\(L = \dfrac{e}{dI/dt} = \dfrac{30}{75} = 0{\cdot}4\) H

Comparing with \(E = E_0\sin\omega t\) and \(I = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)\): \(E_0 = 5{\cdot}0\) V, \(I_0 = 3{\cdot}0\) A, \(\omega = 314\) rad s\(^{-1}\), \(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

**(a)** The current **lags** behind the emf by \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (less than \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)), so the circuit is an LR circuit: the component X is an **inductor**.

**(b)** \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt 2} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}0}{1{\cdot}414} \approx 2{\cdot}12\) A

**(c)** \(\omega = 2\pi f\), so \(f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{314}{2 \times 3{\cdot}14} = 50\) Hz

**(d)** Power factor \(= \cos\phi = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 0{\cdot}5\)

**(e)** Impedance \(Z = \dfrac{E_0}{I_0} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}0}{3{\cdot}0} \approx 1{\cdot}67\,\Omega\) (the same as \(\dfrac{E_{rms}}{I_{rms}}\)).

answers.value: (a) \(r_n = \frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2 n^2}{\pi m Z e^2} \propto n^2\); (b)(1) in the Sun and the stars; (2) mass of nucleons minus mass of nucleus
answers.working:
**(a)** Consider an electron of mass \(m\) and charge \(e\) moving with speed \(v\) in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) circular orbit of radius \(r_n\) around a nucleus of charge \(Ze\).

The electrostatic attraction provides the centripetal force:

\(\dfrac{mv^2}{r_n} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^2}{r_n^2}\), so \(mv^2 r_n = \dfrac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\) ...(1)

Bohr's quantum condition: the angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\):

\(mvr_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), so \(v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi m r_n}\) ...(2)

Substituting (2) in (1):

\(m \times \dfrac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2 m^2 r_n^2} \times r_n = \dfrac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\)

\(r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 h^2 n^2}{\pi m Z e^2}\)

All quantities except \(n\) are constants, so \(r_n \propto n^2\): the radius of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) Bohr orbit varies directly as the square of the principal quantum number.

**(b)(1)** Nuclear fusion takes place continuously in the **core of the Sun and other stars**, where the very high temperature and pressure let hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium.

**(2)** **Mass defect** of a nucleus is the difference between the sum of the masses of its individual nucleons (protons and neutrons) in the free state and the actual mass of the nucleus:

\(\Delta m = [Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n] - M\)

This missing mass appears as the binding energy of the nucleus, \(\Delta m\,c^2\).

answers.value: (a)(1) To produce energy (electricity) by controlled fission; (2) moderator; (3) insert the control rods fully; (b)(1) \(L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}\) only; (2) the electron is bound to the nucleus
answers.working:
**(a)(1)** A nuclear reactor produces energy by a **controlled nuclear fission chain reaction**. The heat is used to generate electricity; reactors are also used to produce radioisotopes for medicine, industry and research, and for research with neutrons.

**(2)** A material that slows down fast moving neutrons is called a **moderator** (for example ordinary water, heavy water or graphite).

**(3)** In an emergency the reactor is shut down by **inserting the control rods** (made of cadmium or boron) fully into the core. They absorb the neutrons, so the chain reaction stops.

**(b)(1)** It means that the electron can revolve only in those orbits in which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\):

\(L = mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), where \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)

The angular momentum cannot take any value in between; it can change only in steps of \(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\).

**(2)** The negative total energy means that the electron is **bound** to the nucleus by the attractive force. It cannot leave the atom on its own; energy equal to the magnitude of its total energy must be supplied to remove it (ionisation energy, for example \(13{\cdot}6\) eV for the ground state of hydrogen).

answers.value: (i) P: holes majority (trivalent impurity); N: electrons majority (pentavalent impurity); (ii) full wave rectifier described; (iii) Zener diode
answers.working:
**(i)**

| P-type semiconductor | N-type semiconductor |
|---|---|
| Made by doping with a trivalent impurity (e.g. boron, aluminium, indium), an acceptor | Made by doping with a pentavalent impurity (e.g. arsenic, phosphorus, antimony), a donor |
| Holes are the majority charge carriers | Free electrons are the majority charge carriers |
| Electrons are the minority carriers | Holes are the minority carriers |

**(ii) Full wave rectifier (labelled diagram):** The AC input is applied to the primary of a centre-tap transformer. The two ends A and B of the secondary are connected to the P sides of two diodes \(D_1\) and \(D_2\). The N sides of both diodes are joined together at point C. The load resistance \(R_L\) is connected between C and the centre tap T of the secondary, and the output is taken across \(R_L\).

**Working:** During the positive half cycle, end A is positive, \(D_1\) is forward biased and conducts while \(D_2\) is reverse biased; current flows through \(R_L\) from C to T. During the negative half cycle, end B is positive, \(D_2\) conducts and \(D_1\) does not; current again flows through \(R_L\) from C to T. So current flows through the load in the same direction in both half cycles.

**Graph:** Plot input voltage against time as a complete sine wave (positive and negative halves). Below it, plot output voltage against time: a series of positive half-sine humps, one for every half cycle, with no gaps and no negative part. The output is unidirectional (pulsating DC) with twice the frequency of the input.

**(iii)** A **Zener diode** (operated in reverse bias in its breakdown region) is used as a voltage regulator.
